newsitem.title: JAPAN: Angry Japan P.M. wants probe over nuclear accident.
newsitem.headline: Angry Japan P.M. wants probe over nuclear accident.

text.p: A furious Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto ordered a raid on operators of Japan's only nuclear fuel reprocessing plant on Wednesday and promised a full probe into a cover-up of the country's worst nuclear accident.
"I am so angry I cannot utter a single word," a shaken Hashimoto told reporters. "We will get third-party consultants to conduct a full probe."

Hashimoto's remarks came after his government ordered Science and Technology Agency inspectors to raid Power Reactor and Nuclear Fuel Development Corporation (PNC) offices. PNC is the sole public firm in charge of reprocessing nuclear fuel.

PNC executives told a news conference late on Tuesday that its officials falsified a formal report about a March 11 explosion at the Tokaimura nuclear complex, which exposed 37 workers to small doses of radiation.
The complex houses Japan's only nuclear fuel reprocessing plant, just 160 km (100 miles) northeast of Tokyo.
The explosion occured at a bituminisation plant inside the complex, designed to harden low-level nuclear waste by mixing it with asphalt for permanent storage in drums.
No one was seriously harmed in the explosion or fallout but the government said it was Japan's worst nuclear accident.
PNC had come under severe criticism for tardiness in alerting local officials, lax fire-fighting plans and outdated equipment, but the latest revelation points to a cover-up.

The report, submitted to the government on March 21, said staff had visually confirmed that a fire had been put out at the plant. The fire flared up again nine hours later causing an explosion which released radiation into the atmosphere.
PNC executives admitted on Tuesday they had lied that the staff had visually confirmed the fire had been doused.

"In fact no one had confirmed that the fire had been put out. The staff at the scene knew this but had thought that there was no way to change the report once it was made official," PNC manager Hiromasa Nakano said.
Nakano said PNC's Tokaimura officials had straightened out the story among themselves to hide the fact.
"I am afraid that what we have done was an organisational conspiracy to cover up this fact," Nakano said.

"I had believed that there were no lies (in the report) this time," PNC chairman Toshiyuki Kondo told Tuesday's news conference. "I deeply regret this. I thought we had learned a lesson at Monju. I am truly sorry for this."

Kondo was referring to a December 1995 accident at PNC's experimental fast-breeder reactor Monju. Four PNC officials have been accused of falsifying a formal report and hiding video tapes of a massive coolant leak at Monju.
There was no fallout at Monju but the plant remains closed.
Science and Technology Agency officials said they were disgusted and questioned the PNC's integrity.
"We are thoroughly disgusted. There are many of us who feel that the PNC should be disbanded altogether," said one agency official, who asked not to be named, on Wednesday.
A Science and Technology Agency spokesman said the Tokaimura report was an official document which PNC was required to submit to the government under law.
"False entries can lead to prosecution," he said.
The Tokaimura complex recycles about 12 percent of spent nuclear fuel from Japan's 50 running commercial nuclear power plants, with the rest reprocessed at French plants.
Tokaimura is at the heart of Japan's long-term goal of supplying half of the country's power needs by nuclear power generation. At present, nuclear plants supply a third of the country's electricity.
